label: GLM-5.3
prompt_text: Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.

messages.content: Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.

message.content:
The feature I was proudest of shipped to the sound of silence.

Two years ago, my team spent four months building an advanced reporting dashboard. Custom filters. Drag-and-drop charts. Scheduled exports. We rebuilt our entire data layer to support it. Our internal demo got actual applause.

Launch day: nothing. Week one: 47 opens across 20,000 users. Ninety days later, fewer than 2% of accounts had ever touched it — and most of them opened it once and never came back.

I remember pulling up the usage report with my PM and just sitting there. Four months. Countless design reviews. A data migration that nearly broke us. And the market's response was a shrug.

Here's the part that stings: we never talked to a single customer before building it.

We had assumptions, sure. "Enterprise buyers want analytics." "Competitors have dashboards, so we need one." "This is obviously valuable." But we never asked the question that mattered: is this a problem anyone actually has?

Meanwhile, the #1 request in our support queue — the one we kept deprioritizing because it felt too "small" — was bulk editing. We shipped it later in a single sprint. Today it's one of the most-used parts of the product.

That flop taught me more than any successful launch ever has:

→ Talk to users before you write code. Not to pitch your idea — to understand their problem. If you can't name five people who have the problem, you don't have a feature. You have a hypothesis.

→ Define success before launch. We never decided what "good" adoption looked like, so we couldn't tell we were failing until we'd already failed.

→ Ship small, learn fast. A two-week prototype would have told us everything four months of building didn't.

→ Your support queue is a roadmap written by your users. They were telling us exactly what to build. We just thought their requests were too boring.

→ Building isn't the hard part. Adoption is. "If you build it, they will come" is a movie quote, not a go-to-market strategy.

The dashboard didn't die entirely. We stripped it down, paired it with real customer conversations, and a niche segment genuinely loves it now. But it found its audience after we started listening — not before.

These days, I get suspicious when a team is excited about a feature but can't recall the last time they watched a user struggle with the problem it solves.

Excitement is easy to generate internally. Evidence only comes from customers.

What's a feature you shipped into the void — and what did it teach you?

---

~420 words. Happy to swap in your actual feature, numbers, and industry details, or adjust the tone (more vulnerable, more data-driven, shorter) if you'd like.
message.reasoning:
The user wants a LinkedIn post about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used. LinkedIn posts have a particular style: usually personal, somewhat vulnerable, often storytelling-driven, with short paragraphs, sometimes emojis, a hook at the beginning, and a takeaway at the end. They often use line breaks heavily for readability.

Let me think about what makes a good LinkedIn post on this topic:

1. **Hook**: Something attention-grabbing. "We spent 4 months building a feature nobody used" or similar.
2. **Story specifics**: Real-feeling details — the feature, the team, the timeline, the launch, the anticipation.
3. **The emotional arc**: excitement → launch day → silence → disappointment → reflection.
4. **The lesson**: The core insight. Common lessons from failed features:
   - Built based on assumptions, not user research
   - Never talked to a single user before building
   - Confused "we can build it" with "people want it"
   - The feature solved a problem nobody had
   - Didn't validate demand first
   - Users don't read changelogs; distribution matters as much as building
   - Launched and expected adoption to happen organically
   - The problem: building in a vacuum

5. **Takeaways**: Practical, actionable lessons others can apply.

The word limit is 500 words. LinkedIn posts are often shorter, but 500 words is the cap. I should aim for something in the 300-450 word range — long enough to tell a story with substance, short enough to feel like a real LinkedIn post.

Let me draft this. I should make it feel authentic — first person, a specific (fictional but plausible) feature, specific numbers, and genuine reflection. I should avoid the clichés that make LinkedIn posts parody-worthy (e.g., "I have a PhD in..." hooks, excessive humility-bragging, "Agree?"), though some LinkedIn conventions are fine (short paragraphs, a takeaway list).

Let me pick a fictional feature: something relatable. Ideas:
- An advanced reporting dashboard that users never opened
- A customizable color/theme feature
- A "smart export" tool
- An internal tool
- A social feature in a productivity app

A good one: a report builder / analytics dashboard — teams often assume users want deep analytics, but most users just want the basics. Or maybe a "templates library" or "saved views."

Let me go with: we built an advanced analytics dashboard with custom reports, filters, export options — took months — and found that 97% of users never opened it; the ones who did, did so once. Meanwhile, the top feature request in support tickets was something trivial we kept deprioritizing.

Actually, a nice twist: the lesson could be that we never watched a single user use the product during those 4 months. Or: we launched it and told no one effectively (buried in a changelog), so distribution failed. Or: the data was there, we just never looked at it — support tickets told us what users wanted and we ignored it in favor of what was exciting to build.

The strongest, most universal lesson: "We fell in love with the solution before validating the problem." Or the two-part lesson: (1) talk to users before building, (2) a launch isn't the finish line — adoption is.

Let me structure:

**Hook**: "We spent 4 months and [X] engineering hours building a feature. 11 people used it." Or "The proudest launch of my career was also our biggest flop."

**Story**: Describe the feature (advanced reporting dashboard), the excitement, the design polish, the internal demo applause, launch day... then the analytics: tiny adoption. One user emailed asking about something else entirely — a small fix that became hugely used.

**Reflection**: What we learned — we never talked to users; we built what was fun to build / what competitors had / what a stakeholder wanted. The "field of dreams" fallacy: build it and they will come.

**Lessons** (bulleted, LinkedIn-style):
- Before writing a line of code, talk to 5 users about the problem
- Ship the smallest version first / prototype
- Define success metrics before launch (what adoption number = keep investing?)
- Launch is day one — plan for distribution, education, iteration
- Watch what users do, not what they say (or: check support tickets — they're a roadmap written by users)

**Closing**: Short, punchy. "Nobody used the dashboard. Everybody uses the fix that took 2 days." Something like that. End with maybe a question to drive engagement (common on LinkedIn, though optional): "What's a feature you shipped into the void?" — that's actually a good engagement hook and fits the platform.

Formatting considerations: LinkedIn posts don't support markdown headers or bold in plain text, but when someone asks me to "write a LinkedIn post," rendering it with some light formatting in my response is fine — the user will paste it as plain text. I'll use plain text conventions: line breaks, maybe emojis sparingly (some posts use them; I'll use very few or none — maybe one or two like 📉 or ✅ for the list). Actually, moderate emoji use is very LinkedIn. I'll keep it tasteful — maybe checkmarks for lessons or none at all. Let me use minimal emojis to keep it classy but authentic.

Word count: aim for ~350-450 words. Let me draft.

The feature I was proudest of shipped to the sound of silence.

Two years ago, my team spent four months building an advanced reporting dashboard. Custom filters. Drag-and-drop charts. Scheduled exports. We rebuilt our entire data layer to support it. Our internal demo got actual applause.

Launch day: nothing. Week one: 47 opens across 20,000 users. Ninety days later, fewer than 2% of accounts had ever touched it — and most of them opened it once and never came back.

I remember pulling up the usage report with my PM and just sitting there. Four months. Countless design reviews. A data migration that nearly broke us. And the market's response was a shrug.

Here's the part that stings: we never talked to a single customer before building it.

We had assumptions, sure. "Enterprise buyers want analytics." "Competitors have dashboards, so we need one." "This is obviously valuable." But we never asked the question that mattered: is this a problem anyone actually has?

Meanwhile, the #1 request in our support queue — the one we kept deprioritizing because it felt too "small" — was bulk editing. We shipped it later in a single sprint. Today it's one of the most-used parts of the product.

That flop taught me more than any successful launch ever has:

→ Talk to users before you write code. Not to pitch your idea — to understand their problem. If you can't name five people who have the problem, you don't have a feature. You have a hypothesis.

→ Define success before launch. We never decided what "good" adoption looked like, so we couldn't tell we were failing until we'd already failed.

→ Ship small, learn fast. A two-week prototype would have told us everything four months of building didn't.

→ Your support queue is a roadmap written by your users. They were telling us exactly what to build. We just thought their requests were too boring.

→ Building isn't the hard part. Adoption is. "If you build it, they will come" is a movie quote, not a go-to-market strategy.

The dashboard didn't die entirely. We stripped it down, paired it with real customer conversations, and a niche segment genuinely loves it now. But it found its audience after we started listening — not before.

These days, I get suspicious when a team is excited about a feature but can't recall the last time they watched a user struggle with the problem it solves.

Excitement is easy to generate internally. Evidence only comes from customers.

What's a feature you shipped into the void — and what did it teach you?
